title: Finding NULLs: ISNULL Blocks the Seek
description: ISNULL(col,0)=0 wraps the column and scans; test col IS NULL directly to use the index. Why it matters: NULL-handling patterns like ISNULL/COALESCE are everywhere in real queries, and this is one of the most common ways they accidentally disable a perfectly good index.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About

This lesson is about a very specific, very common trap: using `ISNULL()` (or its cousin `COALESCE()`) to test whether a column is empty, instead of just asking directly whether it `IS NULL`. It's an easy habit to fall into — `ISNULL(AssignedTo, 0) = 0` reads naturally as "if AssignedTo is null, treat it as 0, and check if it's 0" — but it silently defeats the index on `AssignedTo`, even in a case where the payoff for using that index would be enormous (only 200 unassigned rows out of 200,000 total).

The reason connects directly to the general idea covered in the "function on a column" and "arithmetic on a column" lessons: `ISNULL()` is a function, and the moment you wrap the *column itself* inside a function call before comparing it to something, you've created a brand-new, computed value that doesn't exist anywhere in the index. The index on `AssignedTo` is a sorted list of the actual `AssignedTo` values (including nulls, which SQL Server treats as sitting at one end of the sort order — nulls are considered the "lowest" possible value in an ascending sort, so they cluster together at the start of the index). But `ISNULL(AssignedTo, 0)` produces a different value for every row — either the real `AssignedTo` value, or a substituted `0` if it was null — and that computed result is what's actually being compared to `0`. SQL Server has no pre-built, sorted structure of "what ISNULL(AssignedTo, 0) evaluates to for each row," so once again, it has to visit every row, apply the function, and check the result — a full scan.

What makes this lesson particularly worth internalizing is that the fix isn't just "cheaper" — it's a completely different, much simpler question that gets you the exact same answer without ever needing a function at all. The entire reason someone reaches for `ISNULL()` here is to handle the "what if it's null" case — but SQL already has a first-class, dedicated way to ask exactly that question: `WHERE AssignedTo IS NULL`. There's no function, no substitution, no computed value — `IS NULL` is a direct test the engine can evaluate using the raw column, and because nulls sit together at one end of a sorted index, SQL Server can seek straight to that cluster of null entries instead of scanning the whole table. `AssignedTo = 0` and `AssignedTo IS NULL` are genuinely, completely different questions in SQL (a subtlety worth sitting with: `NULL` doesn't equal anything, not even another `NULL` — you can never write `WHERE AssignedTo = NULL` and have it work, which is exactly *why* people reach for `ISNULL()` as a workaround in the first place), so the real fix here isn't a clever rewrite of the same logic — it's recognizing you were trying to test for null all along, and there's a direct, sargable way to say that.

This matters more broadly because `NULL`-handling shows up constantly in everyday business queries — "orders not yet assigned," "customers without a phone number," "tasks with no due date," "rows where some optional field was never filled in" — and `ISNULL()`/`COALESCE()` are extremely popular tools for handling nulls in general (they're genuinely useful in the `SELECT` list, for display purposes, or in calculations where you want a fallback value). The trap is specifically using them *inside a WHERE clause filter*, on the very column you're trying to search by, where a much simpler and much faster direct null check would do exactly the same job.

There's a slightly deeper lesson buried in here too, one that generalizes past this specific example: whenever you catch yourself wrapping a column in a function purely to handle an edge case (null, a default value, a special sentinel), it's worth pausing and asking "is there a more direct way to express this same condition without touching the column?" Almost always, if the underlying question is really just "is this null," "is this empty," "is this within a range," there's a sargable, function-free way to ask it — you just have to recognize that the function-wrapped version and the direct version are answering the exact same real-world question, and only one of them lets the database use its index.

It's worth explicitly listing a few more shapes of this same trap so you can recognize it in different disguises: `WHERE COALESCE(ShippedDate, '9999-12-31') > GETDATE()` (checking if something is either unshipped or has a future ship date) hides the same problem as `ISNULL`; `WHERE NULLIF(Quantity, 0) IS NOT NULL` is another variant. In every one of these cases, the underlying question being asked is almost always expressible as a direct condition on the raw column — `IS NULL`, `IS NOT NULL`, or a plain comparison — without ever needing to wrap the column in a function first. A good habit when you catch yourself reaching for `ISNULL`/`COALESCE` inside a `WHERE` clause is to pause and ask: "am I using this to provide a fallback display value, or am I actually just trying to test for null?" If it's the latter — which is extremely common — there's almost always a more direct, sargable way to phrase the exact same real-world question, and finding it is usually just a matter of translating "treat null as X, then compare to X" back into its much simpler original form: "is this null."

One more thing worth remembering: this lesson's fix works cleanly specifically because the underlying business question really was 'is this null' in disguise. If you genuinely need to search using a substituted default value for reasons beyond just null-checking (for example, treating multiple different placeholder values as equivalent), a computed column or a rethink of how the data is stored may serve you better than trying to force a function-wrapped WHERE clause to be fast.

As a final sanity check, try reading your rewritten condition back in plain English and confirming it says exactly what you originally meant: "AssignedTo IS NULL" reads as "there is no assignee" -- which is the real business question -- whereas "ISNULL(AssignedTo, 0) = 0" reads as "treat a missing assignee as the number zero, then check if it equals zero," an unnecessarily roundabout way of asking the identical thing. Whenever the direct phrasing and the function-wrapped phrasing describe the same real condition, always prefer the direct one.

## Scenario
A worklist screen shows *unassigned* orders — rows where `AssignedTo IS NULL`. Only 200 of 200,000 orders are unassigned, and `AssignedTo` is indexed, yet the query scans the whole index.

## Why it's slow
The query is written `WHERE ISNULL(AssignedTo, 0) = 0`. Wrapping the column in `ISNULL()` (or `COALESCE()`) is **non-sargable**: SQL Server must evaluate the function for *every* row before it can test the predicate, so it **scans** the entire index instead of seeking.

## What to look for
- In the plan: an **Index Scan** on `IX_Orders_AssignedTo` reading all 200k index rows to return 200.
- In `STATISTICS IO`: hundreds of logical reads for a 200-row result.

## The concept
`NULL`s are stored in the index and sort at its **start**, so the predicate `AssignedTo IS NULL` can **seek** straight to them. Any function around the column — even `ISNULL()` whose only purpose is to test for NULL — throws that away. Use `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL` directly.
startingQuery: SELECT OrderId, CustomerId, OrderDate, Total FROM Orders WHERE ISNULL(AssignedTo, 0) = 0;
hints: Look at the operator on Orders — is it a Scan or a Seek? A function on the column forces a Scan.
ISNULL(AssignedTo, 0) must be computed for every row, so the index key can't be seeked.
Test for NULL directly with the sargable predicate: WHERE AssignedTo IS NULL.
